analysis.one_liner: Removes federal penalties for state-legal marijuana activities and gives those businesses banking and tax rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced with zero cosponsors, until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bring federal law in line with state marijuana laws. It would end federal criminal and civil penalties for marijuana activities that are legal under state or tribal law, let state-legal marijuana businesses use banks and claim normal tax deductions, and allow federal bankruptcy protection. It also creates individual protections: expunging certain federal marijuana convictions, restoring student aid for misdemeanor possession, protecting homes from civil forfeiture, barring deportation for state-legal marijuana conduct, and letting VA and Indian Health Service doctors recommend state marijuana programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Marijuana consumers, patients, and businesses in states where marijuana is legal; veterans and tribal patients whose doctors could recommend state marijuana programs; students with a misdemeanor marijuana possession conviction; immigrants facing deportation for state-legal conduct; renters in federally assisted housing; and people with small federal marijuana convictions seeking to clear their records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, veterans, students, and state-legal cannabis businesses

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates federal regulatory, civil, and criminal penalties under the Controlled Substances Act for marijuana activities authorized by state or tribal law, and for ancillary services like payment processing, advertising, and property leasing.
Amends the tax code so state-legal marijuana businesses can claim federal tax credits and deductions, removing the current rule (Section 280E) that denies them ordinary business deductions.

Bars federal banking regulators from penalizing or discouraging banks and credit unions that serve state-legal marijuana businesses, and immunizes those institutions from federal prosecution for providing the services.
Entitles marijuana-related businesses to federal bankruptcy protection under chapters 7, 11, and 13.
Creates a process to expunge federal criminal records for marijuana offenses where the conduct was legal under state or tribal law, or involved possession of one ounce or less.
Restores federal student aid eligibility for students convicted of a misdemeanor marijuana possession offense, including those currently suspended.

Exempts real property from civil forfeiture for state-authorized marijuana conduct and specifies that state-legal marijuana activity is not 'drug-related criminal activity' under federally assisted housing law.
Bars inadmissibility and deportation for marijuana conduct permitted under state or tribal law.
Authorizes Department of Veterans Affairs and Indian Health Service providers to give medical recommendations about participation in state marijuana programs.
Sets up a separate, faster registration process for medical marijuana research and lifts limits on the number of licensed manufacturers and distributors of research marijuana.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, federal tax revenue would fall modestly because state-legal marijuana businesses could deduct business expenses. Anti-money-laundering oversight would be lighter, since banks would not have to file suspicious-activity reports on compliant marijuana accounts in specified circumstances. Federal drug enforcement agencies would lose their enforcement role over state-legal conduct, and critics of commercial marijuana could argue the advertising provisions normalize marijuana use more broadly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal tax revenue and drug-enforcement agencies

drawbacks.text: Banks would no longer be required to file suspicious-activity reports on marijuana business accounts when the institution reasonably believes the business complies with state law and federal enforcement priorities, easing an existing anti-money-laundering safeguard.

The bill would allow print and broadcast advertising of state-legal marijuana, subject to a bar on ads meant to induce people from states where marijuana is illegal to travel to buy it; broader advertising raises the objection that it increases exposure among people who should not use marijuana.

The expungement process is narrow: it covers only federal convictions, requires a petition, requires the applicant to have fully served the sentence including all fines, and lets the government contest each petition.

A good-faith objection to the whole approach: rather than rescheduling or descheduling marijuana nationally, the bill makes federal law defer to 50 different state and tribal rulebooks, leaving a patchwork where conduct is legal on one side of a state line and a federal crime on the other.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and concrete for the millions of people in states where marijuana is legal: banking access reduces cash-only businesses that are robbery targets, normal tax treatment ends an effective penalty on small businesses, and the individual protections touch students, veterans, immigrants, and people with old convictions. The costs are real but smaller: a modest federal tax revenue loss, lighter anti-money-laundering reporting on a specific set of accounts, and broader advertising. The main honest criticism is design, not cost: it papers over the federal-state conflict rather than resolving it, leaving interstate questions unsettled.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on March 30, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the bill's history; the committee never reported it and the full Senate never considered it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, everyone banking on change kept the status quo: state-legal marijuana businesses kept paying effectively higher taxes and operating largely in cash, banks kept the federal legal risk of serving them, and people with federal marijuana convictions, students, and veterans gained nothing. The existing federal enforcement and tax framework simply continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal status quo; no one new

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; no one joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from the day it was referred in March 2017; never held a hearing or markup and never reported it to the Senate.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman through the 115th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors beyond its Democratic sponsor, so no partisan split appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill gives these businesses normal federal tax deductions, banking access, bankruptcy protection, and advertising rights. Consumers in legal states also benefit because banking access means less cash on hand and lower costs, so the industry's gain runs alongside the public's.

The bill gives depository institutions a legal safe harbor to serve marijuana businesses, making them the permanent channel for the industry's money, while trimming their suspicious-activity reporting duty for compliant accounts. Consumers gain from reduced cash handling but also from the fact that the accounts remain tracked through basic record-keeping requirements.

Federal prosecutors and agencies would lose their criminal, civil, and forfeiture role over state-legal marijuana conduct. The bill would redirect that effort toward the smaller set of conduct that violates both federal and state law.
